items.title: 4.8 Interconversion of potential energy and kinetic energy

source_refs.note: Topic 4.8 with Figs. 4.12 and 4.13 and Examples 4.5 and 4.6 (PDF 87-89, printed 84-86). The exercise (PDF 89-92) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: Consider a body of mass m at rest, at a height h above the surface of the Earth as shown in Fig. 4.12. At position A, the body has P.E. = mgh and K.E. = 0. We release the body and as it falls, we can examine how kinetic and potential energies associated with it interchange.

blocks.alt: A block of mass m at A, height h above the ground C, falls straight down. Arrows give x from A to B, (h - x) from B to C and h from A to C. Beside them: at A, P.E = mgh and K.E = 0; at B, P.E = mg (h - x) and K.E = mgx; at C, P.E = 0 and K.E = mgh.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.12: A body of mass m falling from height h: P.E and K.E at A, B and C (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.12).

blocks.text: Let us calculate P.E. and K.E. at the position B when the body has fallen a distance x, ignoring air friction.
Velocity v_B, at position B, can be calculated from the relation,

blocks.text_alt: as   v_f = v_B ,   v_i = 0 ,   S = x

blocks.text: Total energy at position B = P.E. + K.E.

blocks.text_alt: Total energy = mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh   (4.19)

blocks.text: At position C, just before the body strikes the Earth, P.E. = 0 and K.E. = ½ mv_C², where v_C can be found out by the following expression.

blocks.text_alt: i.e.,   K.E = ½ mv_C² = ½ m × 2gh = mgh

blocks.text: Thus, at point C, kinetic energy is equal to the original value of the potential energy of the body. Actually, when a body falls, its velocity increases i.e., the body is being accelerated under the action of gravity. The increase in velocity results in the increase in its kinetic energy. On the other hand, as the body falls, its height decreases and hence, its potential energy also decreases. Thus, we see (Fig. 4.13) that:

blocks.alt: A falling block of mass m. Its earlier position, drawn dashed, is at height h1 above the ground, where its velocity is v1; at its present position its velocity is v2 and the height of its base is h2.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.13: A falling body with velocity v1 at height h1 and v2 at height h2 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.13).

blocks.text_alt: Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E

blocks.text: where v₁ and v₂ are he velocities of the body at the heights h₁ and h₂ respectively. This result is true only when frictional force is not considered.

If we assume that a frictional force f is present during the downward motion, then a part of P.E. is used in doing work against friction equal to f h. The remaining P.E. = mgh − f h is converted into K.E.

blocks.text_alt: Hence   mgh − f h = ½ mv²
or   mgh = ½ mv² + f h   (4.21)

blocks.latex: \text{Thus}\quad \text{Loss in P.E.} = \text{Gain in K.E.} + \text{Work done against friction}
blocks.text_alt: Thus   Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E. + Work done against friction

blocks.latex: \text{Conversely,}\quad \text{Loss of K.E.} = \text{Gain in P.E.} + \text{Work done against friction}
blocks.text_alt: Conversely,   Loss of K.E. = Gain in P.E. + Work done against friction

blocks.title: Example 4.5
blocks.problem: A car weighing 1100 kg is moving with a velocity of 12 m s⁻¹. When it is at point P, its engine stops. If the frictional force is 120 N, what will be its velocity at point Q? How far beyond Q will it go before coming to rest?
steps: The kinetic energy possessed by the car at point P will partly be converted into P.E. and partly used up in doing work against friction as it reaches point Q. Therefore,
Loss of K.E. = Gain in P.E. + Work against friction
550 kg (144 m² s⁻² − v_f²) = 16170 kg m² s⁻² + 2880 kg m² s⁻²
(144 m² s⁻² − v_f²) = (16170 kg m² s⁻² + 2880 kg m² s⁻²) / 550 kg = 34.6 m² s⁻²
v_f² = 144 m² s⁻² − 34.6 m² s⁻² = 109.4 m² s⁻²
Velocity at point Q, v_f = √(109.4 m² s⁻²) = 10.5 m s⁻¹
Now if the car stops at point R, then using the formula: ½ mv² = fS
½ × 1100 kg × 109.4 m² s⁻² = 120 kg m² s⁻² × S

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the last line the book writes the frictional force as 120 kg m² s⁻². A force of 120 N is 120 kg m s⁻²: ½ × 1100 kg × 109.4 m² s⁻² = 120 kg m s⁻² × S, so S = 60 170 / 120 m ≈ 501 m. The answer is unchanged.

blocks.alt: A road rises in a straight line from P to Q, 24 m along the slope, while Q is 1.5 m higher than P; from Q the road runs level to R. A dotted horizontal line from P and a double arrow at Q mark the 1.5 m rise.
blocks.caption: Example 4.5 (PDF page 88): the road from P up to Q and on to R (original drawing after the textbook's figure in this example).

blocks.title: Example 4.6
blocks.problem: An object of mass 3 kg falls from a height of 15 m. If it strikes the ground with a velocity of 16 m s⁻¹, calculate the average frictional force of the air.
steps: Loss of P.E = Gain in K.E. + Work done against friction
∵ v_i = 0 ,   w h = ½ mv² + f h
3 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 15 m = ½ × 3 kg (16 m s⁻¹)² + f × 15 m
441 kg m² s⁻² = 384 kg m² s⁻² + 15 m × f
blocks.answer: or f = (441 kg m² s⁻² − 384 kg m² s⁻²) / 15 m = 3.8 kg m s⁻² = 3.8 N
